entry.title: ChatGPT or Claude subscription? Run a one-week keep-or-drop test
entry.summary: If you pay for both ChatGPT and Claude, don't decide from one impressive prompt. Give both the same real tasks for a week, record which answers you would actually use, and consider dropping the plan that has no recurring job or feature you would miss. Look at roughly the last two weeks of chats and pick three to five jobs you do again and again: meeting summaries, customer emails, spreadsheet interpretation, code review, research summaries. Skip the clever prompt you tried once. For each job, write down what an acceptable answer must preserve. A meeting summary keeps the agreed dates and the open questions. A delivery email doesn't promise an earlier shipment nobody approved. For a spreadsheet task, work out the expected answer yourself first. Fresh conversations, identical source material…

entry.title: Activate a Desktop App by Scanning a QR Code
entry.summary: A license key is a good credential and a terrible thing to type. On a workstation with a keyboard it is a mild annoyance; on the surfaces where desktop apps increasingly live — a reception kiosk, a digital-signage player, a TV-style app driven by a remote, a locked-down machine where paste is disabled by policy — it is genuinely hostile. A Keyright key is grouped, dash-separated, case-sensitive entropy, typically 25 to 29 characters. Ask someone to enter that with an on-screen keyboard and a D-pad and you have designed a support ticket. The fix is not a shorter key — that would weaken it. The fix is to move key entry off the awkward device entirely. The desktop app displays a QR code; the user scans it with the phone already in their pocket, enters (or pastes) the key there where typing is…

entry.title: Plannotator's Inbox Pattern: Why Background Agent Execution Needs an Email-Like UI
entry.summary: Chat interfaces assume you are present when the agent runs. That assumption breaks when you have three coding agents refactoring a monorepo overnight, a personal assistant drafting emails, and a research agent pulling competitive analysis. You need a review surface that batches decisions, surfaces artifacts, and lets you annotate without blocking execution. It treats agent outputs like email: each task lands in a unified surface where you review diffs, annotate plans, approve prototypes, and send feedback back to the agent. entry.title: Decompiling [UnsafeAccessor]: the extern method with no body and a private name in its attribute
entry.summary: [UnsafeAccessor], added in .NET 8, is the sanctioned way to reach a non-public member without reflection. You declare a static extern method, decorate it with the kind of access you want and the name of the member, and the runtime binds it to the real field, method or constructor at JIT time — no MethodInfo, no delegate, no boxing, and the call site is an ordinary direct call. It is how serializers, test harnesses and parts of the BCL itself reach internals they are entitled to touch without paying the reflection tax. It is also one of the stranger things a decompiler has to read back, because the method it has to reconstruct has no body at all, and the one piece of information that gives it meaning — the name of the private member — lives nowhere except a string inside a custom-attribute …
